title: A Meta-Analysis of the Worked Examples Effect on Mathematics Performance https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-023-09745-1
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), February 21, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Craig Barton's research page summarises a meta-analysis by Christina Areizaga Barbieri, Dana Miller-Cotto, Sarah N. Clerjuste, and Kamal Chawla synthesizing 43 articles (55 studies, 181 effect sizes) on the effectiveness of worked examples for mathematics performance across school years. The analysis finds a medium, positive effect of worked examples on math outcomes compared to non-example-based controls, with students who studied worked examples improving nearly half a standard deviation over those who did not. The authors examine moderators including example correctness, self-explanation prompts, and timing, finding that correct examples were more effective than incorrect ones, and that self-explanation prompts unexpectedly reduced effectiveness rather than enhancing it. Worked examples proved beneficial across a wide range of math domains, especially algebra and geometry. Barton highlights the paper's practical recommendation: wider classroom use of worked examples, paired with professional development in how to construct them for students' needs. The findings are specific to mathematics, and the authors call for further research into how to design effective self-explanation prompts.
points: Worked examples produce a medium positive effect on math learning across school years, with students improving nearly half a standard deviation compared to non-example controls.
Correct worked examples are more effective than incorrect examples used alone or alongside correct ones.
Adding self-explanation prompts to worked examples can be unnecessary or even detrimental to their effectiveness, contrary to common assumption.
Worked examples are effective across math domains but especially strong in algebra and geometry.
The study recommends wider classroom use of worked examples plus teacher professional development in constructing them.
quotes: Worked examples in their various forms are a useful and effective tool to implement in mathematics classrooms, with some forms (i.e., correct examples) being potentially more effective than others (e.g., incorrect examples) and some supplemental features (i.e., self-explanation prompts) being not necessary or even detrimental to their effectiveness of student performance

The study recommends more widespread use of worked examples in mathematics classrooms as well as professional development for teachers in how to create and use their own worked examples based on their students' needs as a practical next step

Worked examples have a positive and moderate effect on student's mathematics learning across school years. Learners who study worked examples improve almost half a standard deviation in their mathematics performance compared to those who do not
Worked examples are a beneficial tool for teaching mathematics across a wide range of mathematics domains, especially algebra and geometry
Correct examples seem to be more effective than incorrect examples alone or in combination with correct examples
The inclusion of self-explanation prompts with examples may not be necessary or even detrimental to their effectiveness on student performance
This research paper is a meta-analysis examining the effectiveness of worked examples on mathematics performance across various educational levels
